BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, shader foundations, 33 terms for shaders in Go-Doh from the pipeline and its built-ins to uniforms and color curves. The exact word lets you tell an AI coding agent precisely what to build.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often think the vertex shader colors the pixels. It does not. A vertex shader runs once per corner and decides where that corner lands. Color is the fragment shader's job once per pixel. Shaders are full of lookalike pairs like that one. This film goes through the terms each one shown so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Seven labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Editor or docs, the term comes from the editor itself or its official documentation. Video only, the term comes from a video lecture and is not in the course text or on the term list, computed. The numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 33 terms about shaders, the small programs that decide where things land and what color each pixel gets in four groups. The first group is what a shader is. Shader, vertex shader, fragment shader, programmable stage, fixed function, rasterization, fragment, varying and interpolation.

B0102.heard: The second group is the Godot language. Godot shading language, shader type, canvas item, spatial, compile error, UV, screen UV, vertex color, texture, color and time. This is what you write and what Godot hands your program to read.

B0103.heard: The third group is steering from code, uniform, hint range, source color, material, shader material, set shader parameter and shared material. These terms say how a script sets the values of shader uses.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is color and curves. RGBA, linear versus SRGB, mix, step, smooth, step, and clamp. These are the numbers a fragment shader turns into a color.

B0201.heard: A grid of small squares fills with color. A shader is a small program that runs on the graphics processor, many copies at once. Here one program runs 384 times once per cell, and each run works out its color from its own position. No run can look at another run's result. For example, the failure flash in the Walker game is a shader. The same few lines run for every pixel of Claude, the player character.

B0202.heard: Now nine dots ride a wave. A vertex shader runs once per vertex, a corner of the geometry, and decides where that corner lands. Nine vertices, nine runs. Each dot is lifted by a sign of time, so the line waves and no pixel color is decided here. For example, a flag at the end of a level could wave because a vertex shader moves its corners up and down a little on every frame.

B0203.heard: A disk of pixels fills in one cell at a time. A fragment shader also called a pixel shader runs once for each pixel the mesh covers and decides that pixel's color. Here it ran for all 156 pixels with a pale glint across the middle. The vertex shader moves corners and the fragment shader colors pixels. For example, tinting claw toward dark ink when a run fails is fragment shader work. Nothing moves, only colors change.

B0301.heard: This is the pipeline one triangles journey from top to bottom. A programmable stage is a step of the pipeline where you supply the program by writing a shader for it. Two of the four stages are yours, lit in red, the vertex shader, and the fragment shader. For example, when you ask an AI coding agent for a glow on a coin, the shader code it writes runs in those two stages and nowhere else.

B0302.heard: Now the other two boxes are lit. Fix function means a step that is built in. You can set its options, but you cannot program it. The name comes from older graphics hardware where every step worked like this. Here two of the four are built in rasterization and blending with the depth test. For example, choosing an additive blend for a fire sprite so it brightens what is behind it, is picking an option, not writing code.

B0303.heard: The triangle now sits on a grid of screen cells. Rasterization is the built-in step that turns a triangle into fragments, one for every screen cell who center lies inside it. The Vertex shader gave three corners. Rasterization gives the cells 89 out of 384. For example, when a platform sprite is drawn, rasterization works out which screen pixels it covers before any fragment shader gives them a color.

B0304.heard: The pipeline is drawn again now with fragment shaders A, B and C. A scene can use many fragment shaders, one for each material, plus extra passes that work on the 2D image already drawn. For example, each sprite in a level can carry its own fragment shader, and one more pass can then turn the whole finished frame gray.

B0401.heard: The same triangle with its covered cells in gray. A fragment is a candidate pixel color. Rasterization makes one for each screen position the triangle covers and each one waits for the fragment shader to give it a color. It is only a candidate because later steps decide what reaches the screen. Here there are 89. For example, where the player sprite overlaps a wall, both make fragments for the same pixels and blending decides what you finally see.

B0402.heard: Each corner now holds a color, red, green and blue. A varying is a value the vertex stage writes at each corner and passes onto the fragment stage, blended on the way. One varying three values. The uniform is the same for the whole draw and a varying changes across the triangle. For example, a vertex shader for a hill can write each corner's height into a varying, so the fragment shader shades the low ground darker.

B0403.heard: Every covered cell now has a blended color. Interpolation in the shader sense means blending the corner value smoothly across the triangles fragments. Each fragment takes a mix weighted by how near it is to each corner. The outline cell has weights of 0.32, 0.44, and 0.23. For example, a sky drawn as one big rectangle, dark blue at the top corners and pale at the bottom ones. Gets a smooth gradient from interpolation alone.

B0501.heard: A table of the six shader types and a short shader below it. The shader type line is the first line of every go-dough shader. It says what the program draws and so which functions you may write after it. Here it says canvas item and a fragment function follows. For example, the failure flash for Claude begins with shader type canvas item because Walker is a 2D game.

B0502.heard: The canvas item row is lit and a red box moves across a 2D canvas. Canvas item is the Godo shader type for 2D drawing which means sprites, shapes in the UI, the user interface. You may write vertex, fragment and light functions. A corner is two numbers and pixels here 20 and 70. For example, a shader that makes a health bar pulse on screen would be a canvas item shader.

B0503.heard: Now the spatial row is lit and a wire cube turns in 3D space. Spatial is the Godot shader type for 3D meshes. A corner now has three numbers, here one 0.4 and 1.36. Canvas item draws 2D and spatial draws 3D. For example, a coin modeled in Blender and placed in a 3D level would get its shine from a spatial shader.

B0601.heard: A five-line shader with a note beside each line. The Godo shading language is the language every Godo shader is written in. It is based on GLSL, the open GL shading language, but simplified. Types such as float and the word uniform come from GLSL, while color and the fragment function are Godo's own names. For example, a glow you learn to write in another engine carries over. Because the ideas are the same and only the dialect changes.

B0602.heard: Same shader with one semicolon deleted from line 4. A compile error means the shader fails to build, and Godot writes an error message here shader error expected a semicolon. In this simulated run, as in the real headless runs it copies the run still exits with code 0. A compile error is rejected while a wrong look builds fine. For example, an agent can drop a semicolon from Claude's flash shader, and the test still passed though the shader never built.

B0603.heard: Two more lines appear under the log. The uniform list comes back empty because the shader did not parse and the run's exit code is zero so nothing failed. Only the log line or that empty list shows the compile error. For example, a test you write for shader should check that its uniform list holds the names you expect and fail when the list is empty.

B0701.heard: A checkerboard texture of 8x8 tiles on a square, with a probe moving over it. UV is a pair of coordinates that maps a surface to a texture. U runs left to right and V runs top to bottom, both from 0 to 1, whatever the size of the surface. The probe stops at 0.5 across and 0.8 down. For example, a coin sprite drawn small or large reads the same pixel of its picture at the same UV.

B0702.heard: Two copies of the square sit at different places on one screen. Screen UV is the position of the current fragment on the screen from zero to one. Both probes share the same UV, but the left one is zero point two four across the screen and the right one zero point seven nine. UV is the position on the surface. Screen UV the position on the screen. For example, a vignette that darkens the corners of the screen is worked out from screen UV.

B0801.heard: A strip of terrain with a colored dot at each vertex. Vertex color is a color stored on each vertex and blended across the face, the way a varying is. Here each color comes from the vertex's height, green when low and gray when high. The heights are made up for the picture. For example, Claude in the Walker game has no image at all. His terracotta body color is carried as vertex color by the rectangles that draw him.

B0802.heard: A small texture on the left and the same picture drawn as a sprite on the right. Texture is the Godot built in that holds the default 2D texture the item was drawn with its image. Reading it a UV returns one textle, here textle 1, 3, of a made up 4x4 texture. For example the fragment shader on a coin sprite can read texture at UV to get the coin's own picture before it tints at gold.

B0803.heard: Three rows of color sums. Color arrives in the fragment function holding vertex color times the texture color, and whatever you leave in it is drawn. A sprite with an image keeps its image. Claude with no image keeps his vertex color, but read only the texture and his color is dropped and he comes out white. For example, an agent that copies a sprite tutorial and starts Claude's flash from the texture turns him white. Starting from color keeps him terracotta.

B0804.heard: Sign wave over 10 seconds and a color swatch that pulses with it. Time is Godo's built-in clock, the second since the engine started, and it wraps back to zero after 3600 seconds one hour. At 10 seconds the mix amount here is 0.96. Time is not the time since your own event. For example, a coin can shimmer forever from time alone, but a flash when the player dies needs code that knows when the death happened.

B0901.heard: A small made up sprite with a slider under it. The uniform, also called a shader parameter, is a value set from code that stays the same for every pixel of one draw. It is how a script steers a shader. Here the script sets flash amount to 0.5 and the body and the eyes both move halfway toward Dark Inc. For example, the walker flash uses a uniform named flash amount, which the player's script sets on every frame.

B0902.heard: Two sliders, hint range gives a uniform a slider in the inspector and the slider stops at its end here one. It does not clamp a value set from code. Code set 7 and 7 is stored so the body's red channel works out minus 1067 far outside 0 to 255. For example, if a power-up script pushes a glow uniform past its range, the hint will not catch it. Clamp the value in the script first.

B0903.heard: Five pairs of bars and SRGB value above its linear value. Source color is a hint that marks a uniform as a color in SRGB. The encoding of colors people picked by eye, so Godo can decode it to linear before the maths. In 2D, not always. An SRGB 0.5 is only 0.214 in linear, for example. A tint color you pick in the inspector for a lava floor in a 3D level should be marked source color.

B1001.heard: One shader file feeds two boxes. A material is a shader together with its parameter values and textures. A shader material is the kind of material that uses your own custom shader and holds its values. The shader alone has no values. Here one flash shader gives a terracotta look at zero and dark ink at one. For example, two crystals can share one glow shader and differ only in their materials. And Walker's player script builds a shader material to give Claude his flash.

B1002.heard: Two calls, one above the other. Set shader parameter changes one uniform's value on a material found by its name and the name is a plain string. The top call misspells flash amount, so nothing matches, no error appears and the value stays zero. The bottom call spells it right and the value becomes one. For example, if an agent types a coin's sparkle uniform with the wrong capital letter, the sparkle never shows and nothing in the log says why.

B1003.heard: Three squares two join to one material and one with its own. A shared material is one material used by many objects, so a change to it hits them all. Setting flash amount to one on the shared material darkens two nodes together. The third node C keeps zero because it has its own duplicated copy. For example, if every coin in a level shares one material, making one coin flash makes them all flash unless that coin gets its own copy.

B1101.heard: Claude's body color sits over a checkerboard with four channel bars beside it. RGBA means red, green, blue and alpha and alpha is opacity. When it's solid and zero is see-through. Here alpha has settled at 0.5 so the checkerboard shows through and the red channel over white comes out at 238. For example, a ghost enemy drawn at half alpha lets the level behind it show through, while it's red, green and blue stay the same.

B1102.heard: A curve from sRGB values to linear values. Linear versus sRGB are two ways to hold a color. sRGB is the encoding for images shown to people with steps spaced for the eye. Linear values are proportional to light, the right space for maths. Halfway up the sRGB scale is only 0.214 of the light. For example, when a lamp lights a 3D room, the light is added up in linear. And the result is encoded to sRGB for the screen.

B1201.heard: A straight red line with a color strip underneath. Mix blends two values by a fraction and is also called lerp. At zero you get the first value at one the second and a straight line between. Here mix of 0.2 and 0.9 at an input of 0.62 gives 0.63. For example, a health bar that fades from green toward red as the player loses health is a mix of the two colors.

B1202.heard: Now the red line jumps. Step with an edge gives zero below the edge and one from the edge up. A hard switch with nothing in between. Here the edge is 0.5 so an input of 0.62 gives 1. For example, a shader that draws the filled part of a health bar can use step so each pixel is either full color or empty with a sharp boundary.

B1203.heard: The red line is now an S. Smooth step rises from 0 to 1 between two edges along a smooth S curve. It is a step with a ramp. Here the edges are 0.25 and 0.75 and 0.62 gives 0.83. Step is a hard switch and smooth step eases. For example, the soft edge of a circle of torchlight in a dark cave level is a smooth step on the distance from its center.

B1204.heard: A dashed line runs off the top and bottom, and the red line is cut flat at both ends. Clamp holds a value inside a minimum and a maximum. The dashed line is the input, and the red line is the result held between 0.1 and 0.9. Here 0.62 gives 0.69. For example, Walker's player script clamps the flash amount between 0 and 1 before the shader ever sees it.

B1301.heard: Each pair sets two look alike terms side by side. On the left, a vertex shader runs per vertex and moves corners, here seven of them. On the right, a fragment shader runs per pixel and sets color, here 21 pixels.

B1302.heard: A uniform is one value for the whole draw. Every cell on the left shows the same amount, one. A varying changes across the face. On the right it runs from zero on the left to one on the right.

B1303.heard: A shader is the program and it holds no values. On the left, the flash shader file code only. A material is the shader plus its values. On the right, the same file with flash amounts set to one and its dark color.

B1304.heard: Hint range only shapes the slider and clamps nothing. On the left, a value of 1.5 set from code stays 1.5. Clamp limits the value in the code. On the right, after clamp, it is 1.

B1401.heard: A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it beside a chart of what it does. Make the edge glow smoothly becomes U smooth step from 0.3 to 0.7. The gray step jumps. The red smooth step eases over the same edge.

B1402.heard: Make the flag wave becomes in the vertex function, add 20 times the sign of time times 3, plus the x position times 0.05 to each vertex's height. Half a second later, from gray to red, the peaks have moved 30 pixels.

B1403.heard: Tint it halfway becomes mixed color toward the flash color by 0.5. The body 221, 119, 91, becomes 129, 86, 83. The blue is really 82 and a half rounded up.

B1404.heard: Let the script control it becomes, declare Flash Amount as a uniform with hint range 0-1, and clamp the value in the script before set shader parameter. From code 1.5 clamps to 1, the hint alone leaves it at 1.5.

B1405.heard: The colors look washed out becomes Mark color uniform source color. So sRGB values can be decoded to linear before the maths. In 2D not always an sRGB value of 0.5 is 0.214 of the light. Used as linear it is far too bright.

B1501.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a shade or an AI coding agent wrote. First, does this code run per vertex or per pixel? That tells you whether it moves corners or sets colors.

B1502.heard: Second, does it compile with no shader error line in the log? A broken shader can still leave the run's exit code at zero, so read the log or check the uniform list.

B1503.heard: Third is each uniform spelled the same in the script and in the shader. A misspelled name and set shader parameter does nothing and raises no error.

B1504.heard: Fourth is the range enforced in code and not only by hint range. The slider stops at its end, but a value set from code is stored as given.

B1505.heard: Fifth are colors marked source color with the maths done in linear. A color picked by I is SRGB. Source color asks Godot to decode it before the maths. In 2D that does not always happen.

B1506.heard: Sixth, which rules can a machine prove in which need your own eyes, a headless test can prove the shader parsed. Only a person looking at the screen can judge the look, then say it exactly. Not make it glow, but smooth step from 0.3 to 0.7.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap a vertex shader moves corners and a fragment shader colors pixels. Rasterization makes fragments and a varying is blended across them. A compile error can still leave the runs exit code at zero. The uniform is set from code and hint range does not clamp it. A shader is the program and a material is the shader plus its values. Step switches hard at its edge and smooth step eases between two edges.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on Godot shader terms with short game-making cases one at a time. Use the terms Vertex shader, Fragment shader, varying uniform, hint range, clamp material, shared material, step and smooth step. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms Shader Foundations at Nick Bear Brown.
